title: Defects of Bohr's Theory — Quick Revision List
notes: A compressed revision list of Bohr's defects, each with its one-line reason — the fast recall version. The fully argued list is in the main defects note.
1. **One-electron only** — electron–electron repulsion and screening (Z_eff) are ignored; fails for He, Li, all multi-electron atoms.
2. **No fine structure** — no relativity, no spin; cannot explain doublets (Na D 589.0/589.6 nm; Hα doublet).
3. **No Zeeman/Stark splitting** — no magnetic quantum number or orbital magnetic moment; cannot explain splitting in magnetic/electric fields.
4. **No line intensities or selection rules** — gives possible wavelengths, not probabilities of transitions.
5. **Contradicts the uncertainty principle** — definite r and p simultaneously is impossible (Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π); orbits cannot be real trajectories.
6. **Ignores wave–particle duality** — treats the electron as a particle in a path; de Broglie/Schrödinger replace orbits by orbitals.
7. **Ad hoc postulates** — mvr = nh/2π is imposed, not derived (de Broglie's standing waves later justified it).
8. **No probability, no chemistry** — cannot give electron density, orbital shapes, subshell structure, bonding or molecular spectra; only the crude Bohr–Bury scheme for periodicity.

1916 Sommerfeld (elliptical orbits, azimuthal quantum number → fine structure) → 1924 de Broglie (matter waves) → 1925 Pauli/Uhlenbeck–Goudsmit (spin) → 1926 Schrödinger (wave equation, orbitals) → 1927 Heisenberg (uncertainty). Each repair targets one defect above.
confusion: ❌ Bohr's theory failed completely. ✅ It is exact for one-electron species (H, He⁺) — defects appear only beyond that scope.
❌ Fine structure needs many electrons. ✅ It comes from spin and relativity even in hydrogen.
❌ Defect 5 means measurements are inaccurate. ✅ It is a fundamental limit of nature, not an instrument problem.

universalFacts: Sodium D lines 589.0/589.6 nm — the standard fine-structure exhibit.
Sommerfeld's elliptical orbits introduced the azimuthal quantum number l in 1916.
Schrödinger's 1926 equation removed orbits in favour of orbitals and repaired every defect at once.
examples: **Problem:** Why can Bohr's model not predict the relative brightness of Hα and Hβ? **Solution:** intensities depend on transition probabilities (population of levels and dipole strengths) — concepts absent from the model; quantum mechanics supplies them.

summary: A compressed revision list of the eight defects of Bohr's theory, each with its one-line physical reason: (1) valid only for one-electron species, since electron–electron repulsion and screening are ignored; (2) no fine structure, because the model has neither relativity nor spin; (3) no Zeeman or Stark splitting, for want of a magnetic quantum number; (4) no line intensities or selection rules; (5) it contradicts the uncertainty principle, since a Bohr orbit fixes r and p at once; (6) it ignores wave–particle duality; (7) the postulates are ad hoc, being imposed rather than derived; and (8) it gives no probability, no orbital shapes and no chemistry. The rescue sequence is Sommerfeld (1916), de Broglie (1924), spin (1925), Schrödinger (1926) and Heisenberg (1927), each step repairing one defect.
importantConcepts: Defect 1 — one-electron species only: e⁻–e⁻ repulsion and screening (Z_eff = Z − S) are ignored
Defects 2 and 3 — no fine structure (needs relativity and spin) and no Zeeman/Stark splitting (needs the magnetic quantum number)
Defects 4 and 5 — no line intensities or selection rules, and the definite orbit violates Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π
Defects 6–8 — no wave–particle duality, ad hoc postulates, and no probability density, orbital shapes or chemistry
Rescue timeline: Sommerfeld 1916 → de Broglie 1924 → spin 1925 → Schrödinger 1926 → Heisenberg 1927
importantStatements: Bohr's theory is exact for one-electron species (H, He⁺); the defects appear only beyond that scope.
Fine structure comes from spin and relativity even in hydrogen, so it is not a many-electron effect.
The uncertainty principle is a fundamental limit of nature, not an instrumental defect.
The quantisation rule mvr = nh/2π was postulated; de Broglie's standing waves later derived it.
Schrödinger's 1926 equation removed orbits in favour of orbitals and repaired every defect at once.

keyPoints: Order for the answer: one-electron limit → fine structure → Zeeman/Stark → intensities → uncertainty → duality → ad hoc → chemistry.
Sodium D lines 589.0/589.6 nm are the standard fine-structure exhibit.
Sommerfeld's elliptical orbits (1916) introduced the azimuthal quantum number l.
Only the Bohr–Bury 2n² scheme was available for periodicity — the crudest part of the picture.
specialNotes: Defect 5 does not mean measurements are inaccurate; it means a trajectory is not a physical object.
Zeeman needs a magnetic field and a magnetic quantum number; Stark needs an electric field — do not swap the names.
Even after de Broglie justifies the quantisation, the orbit picture still carries a definite trajectory, so it is a bridge, not the answer.
examShortTricks: Give each defect as 'defect — reason' in one line; bare lists score poorly.
Never mix this list with the limitations of Rutherford's model — examiners check scope.
Attach a name to each repair: Sommerfeld, de Broglie, Schrödinger, Heisenberg.
examNotes: This revision list is aimed at the 4–5 mark 'state the defects with reasons' question.
One-mark items usually name a single effect (Zeeman, fine structure) and ask which model fails.
A 2-mark numerical comparison such as r₁(He⁺) = 0.2645 Å versus r₁(H) = 0.529 Å is common.
